newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-Australia's Colly Cotton sees bonanza.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-Australia's Colly Cotton sees bonanza.

text.p: Australia's largest cotton producer and the world's second largest integrated cotton company, Colly Cotton Ltd, announced its stock exchange float plans on Monday, forecasting massive rises in profit and output.

It said the end of the worst Australian drought in 100 years, the cheap purchase of new cotton farms during the drought and the world-wide expansion of its marketing operations would almost double forecast cotton sales in the current year.

"During the worst drought this century, management focused on strategies to ensure production could be maintained and is now in a position to benefit from potential increases brought about by improved conditions," Colly Cotton managing director David Farley said.
Colly Cotton's current owner, Commonwealth Funds Management (CFM), said 107 million shares would be issued to the public at A$1.00 each, representing 50 percent of the company.
CFM said its unitholders would take up 25 percent of the shares on offer and the Argentinian-based Kalhbetzer group would also buy 25 percent.
The offer would open on September 30, close on October 18 and share trading should start on October 30.

Colly Cotton said in the float prospectus it expected cotton production from its own farms would surge to 180,700 bales in the year to June 30, 1997 from 22,400 in calendar 1995 and 40,200 in the six months to June 30, 1996.

Total cotton sales, including the marketing of cotton grown by others in Australia and elsewhere, were forecast to rise to 839,400 bales in 1996/97 from 429,200 bales in calendar 1995 and 245,800 bales in the six months to June 30.
Net profit would jump in tandem to A$21.43 million (US$16.95 million) in 1996/97 from A$0.69 million in calendar 1995 and A$1.23 million in the six months to June 30, 1996.
Colly Cotton forecast that it would produce about 20 percent of Australia's cotton crop in the current year.
Australia produces about two percent of total world output, but because 90 percent of the crop is exported, it is the world's third largest exporter behind the United States and Uzbekistan.
Colly Cotton said it had set up cotton marketing operations in the United States and internationally to help offset the weather-related risk linked to its Southern Hemisphere Australian production.
It said it was the second largest integrated cotton company in the world behind the privately held Boswell operation in California.

Farley said Australian cotton exporters were unique in the world scene in that they were not supported by government subsidies as in the United States or a quasi-government, quasi-Mafia operation like those in Uzbekistan.
"We find ourselves between the shotgun and the (subsidised cotton) case sometimes," he said.
Farley said Colly Cotton also eyed expansion within the Australian industry which would continue to be rationalised.
He also said the company's production forecasts were conservative and the outlook for world cotton prices was firm.
"If the sun shines and everything works, we should be able to beat them," Colly Cotton managing director David Farley told reporters.
"We're well out of drought. The water outlook looks good,"
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
